implementation_notes: The canonical Rust realization is a tuple struct with a single field: it creates a new type rather than an alias, is a zero-cost abstraction, and privacy keeps the inner value reachable only through the code you write. Derive the value traits (Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Debug) and add repr(transparent) when the ABI or FFI matters; put validation in an associated parse/TryFrom and keep the field private so UserId (the tuple constructor) is not callable from outside the module. The pattern doubles as the only legal way to implement a foreign trait for a foreign type.
pitfalls: A pub field or a pub tuple constructor defeats the pattern: keep the field private and expose get/into_inner deliberately, otherwise UserId(raw) is legal everywhere.
Deriving or hand-writing traits inconsistently (Hash without Eq, PartialEq without Eq) makes HashMap/BTreeMap behaviour differ per wrapper type.
Serde treats a tuple struct as a newtype in most formats but #[serde(transparent)] is the explicit contract; without it, a change of shape silently changes the wire format.

variants.name: nutype derive macro (validated newtype)
variants.implementation_notes: When the wrapper must sanitise and validate its value and stay valid through deserialization, the nutype proc macro generates the newtype, the checked constructor and the serde/TryFrom plumbing from one attribute list, making an invalid value unconstructible - including from JSON. Use it when many validated primitives would otherwise repeat TryFrom and deserializer impls; keep the plain tuple struct when the type has no invariant or the project avoids proc macros.
pitfalls: The guarantees hold only for the generated constructors: a hand-written From/Deserialize impl added later reopens the hole the macro closed.
Proc macros expand at build time, so errors are reported at the attribute site and IDE support lags; the crate also adds a build-time dependency to the model layer, which some workspaces forbid.
